rv.q: It's an intellectually fascinating gambit...a crisis that proves to be a lot to handle
Mona Pirnot's 'I Love You So Much I Could Die' is a closed, solipsistic box.

I can see some theatergoers dismissing the way Pirnot and Hnath tell her story as gimmicky; avant-garde affectation. Even the design, which is a kind of anti-design – Mimi Lien’s set no set, just the brick walls of the stage, and the desk in the middle – could reinforce that impression.

Pirnot’s performance—apart from her quiet, almost self-effacing singing—could itself be performed by a robot, so there’s no way to comment on it. On the other hand, the artificial voice has a kind of hypnotic effect that—because of its mechanical quality—lands a few funny remarks in a way that would likely have eluded a more committed human voice.
There's a recessive, second-hand quality to Mona Pirnot's solo performance piece
I'm not convinced that this is the best way to share this deeply personal narrative.
